mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

content.content:
> Inference Endpoints, GPU Compute, AI Workflows, and Agent Deployment
- [Inference Overview](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/inference-engine/ie-intro.md): Serverless and Dedicated endpoints for running ML models in production on GMI Cloud.
- [Dedicated Endpoint](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/inference-engine/marketplace/dedicated.md): Provision a private inference endpoint for a chosen model with reserved GPU capacity.
- [Playground](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/inference-engine/playground.md): Interactive testbed for every model in the catalog. Chat with LLMs, run multimodal models, and launch workflows.
- [My Models](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/inference-engine/my-models.md): Manage user-owned, fine-tuned, or custom models that your dedicated deployments can target.
- [Fine-Tuning](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/cluster-engine/fine-tuning.md): Fine-tuning support for GMI Cloud models. Coming soon.
- [Reve Create](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/gmi-studio/nodes/image/reve-create.md): Generates an image from a text prompt using the Reve text-to-image model.
- [Kling Text-to-Video](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/gmi-studio/nodes/video/kling-text-to-video.md): Generates a video from a text prompt using Kling models (Standard/Pro, multiple versions).
- [Minimax Hailuo Video](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/gmi-studio/nodes/video/minimax-hailuo-video.md): Generates video using Minimax-Hailuo model (text-to-video or image-to-video).
- [Vidu Q2 Pro I2V](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/gmi-studio/nodes/video/vidu-q2-pro-i2v.md): Generates a video from a single reference image using VIDU Q2 Pro I2V model.
- [Vidu Q2 Pro R2V](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/gmi-studio/nodes/video/vidu-q2-pro-r2v.md): Generates video from multiple reference images and/or videos using VIDU Q2 Pro R2V model.

content.text:
Checked GMI Cloud's own documentation. Short answer: **not built in, but possible if you run your own server on their GPUs.**

## What GMI Cloud offers (from their docs)

| Feature | Per-user LoRA? | Details |
|---|---|---|
| **Serverless endpoints** | ❌ | Their catalog models only |
| **Dedicated Endpoint + "My Models"** | ⚠️ not documented | "Bring your own model. Deploy fine-tuned or proprietary weights." Each deployment reserves its own GPUs. **LoRA and multi-LoRA aren't mentioned anywhere.** |
| **Fine-tuning** | ❌ | The docs page says "**Coming soon**" |
| **GPU Compute** (managed Kubernetes, containers, bare metal) | ✅ **build it yourself** | Raw GPUs: you run vLLM with multi-LoRA (`--enable-lora`) and train adapters yourself |

## Two ways to use GMI

**1. Dedicated Endpoint with one model per user: ❌ not viable at scale**
- You'd merge each user's LoRA into a full copy of the model and deploy each copy.
- That means **one GPU deployment per user**: 1,000 users means 1,000 endpoints, and the cost explodes.
- It only makes sense for one large enterprise customer with its own deployment.

**2. GPU Compute + your own vLLM: ✅ works**
```
GMI GPU container/K8s
  vLLM --model Qwen3-Coder… --enable-lora --max-loras N
  adapters: user-a, user-b, team-x …  (one base model, shared)
  + training jobs (PEFT/Unsloth) on the same GPUs
```
- This is the "self-host vLLM" option from the earlier plan; GMI is just the GPU provider.
- ✅ A unique LoRA per user on one GPU, any base model, training on the same GPUs.
- ❌ You handle running it: scaling, idle GPU cost, cold starts, and loading adapters.

## Compared with the managed options
| | Managed multi-LoRA | Fine-tuning API | Ops effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Together / Fireworks** | ✅ | ✅ | low |
| **GMI Cloud** | ❌ (DIY on GPU Compute) | ❌ (coming soon) | high |
| **Modal / RunPod** | ❌ (DIY) | ❌ (DIY) | medium–high |

**Recommendation:**
- **Pilot:** Together or Fireworks. Multi-LoRA and fine-tuning are ready-made, so you can test whether LoRA helps without running servers.
- **Later:** GMI makes sense if their GPU prices beat Modal or RunPod and you're ready to run vLLM yourself.
- **Ask GMI support first:** "Do Dedicated Endpoints accept LoRA adapters on a shared base model, or let us pass vLLM `--enable-lora` flags?" If yes, it becomes a strong option. The docs don't say.

Sources:
- [GMI Cloud: Inference Overview](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/inference-engine/ie-intro)
- [GMI Cloud: My Models](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/inference-engine/my-models.md)
- [GMI Cloud: Dedicated Endpoint](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/inference-engine/marketplace/dedicated.md)
- [GMI Cloud: Fine-Tuning (coming soon)](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/cluster-engine/fine-tuning.md)
- [GMI Cloud: GPU Compute](https://docs.gmicloud.ai/cluster-engine/index.md)
- [Together: multi-LoRA deployment](https://docs.together.ai/docs/post-training/deployment)
- [Nebius: deploy custom LoRA](https://docs.tokenfactory.nebius.com/fine-tuning/deploy-custom-model)

I ran one search. It found solid numbers for Opus 5.5 on SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 4.0, and some open-weight SWE-bench Pro scores. It found no open-weight Terminal-Bench comparison.

**Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic-reported):** It scores 89.9% on SWE-bench Pro and 66.4% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at xhigh effort, per the system card, and it leads Anthropic's own table on both (Opus 5.5 system card). The Terminal-Bench figure is the Anthropic's Terminal-Bench 4.0 figure, which jumps 14.1 points over Opus 5.

**Independent checks disagree on Terminal-Bench:** Artificial Analysis measured Opus 5.5 at 59.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, a gap of about 6.8 points from Anthropic's number. Another aggregator lists 87.6% (Vals AI) on Terminal-Bench 2.1, which is a different benchmark version, so it isn't directly comparable.

**Open-weight models on SWE-bench Pro:** These are vendor-aggregated numbers from llm-stats, as of September 2026. GLM-5.2 scores 62.1%, Qwen3.8-27B 61.7%, Qwen3.7 Max 60.6%, MiniMax M3 59.0%, Kimi K2.6 58.6%, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max 55.4%. 4. **The gap to Claude comes from model size and training, not personalisation.** The profile and handover help any model work your way, but they won't close a 20-point gap.

No, nothing has been removed yet. Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B is still the default local model in the code (`config.py`: `MODEL = "mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct-4bit"`). Everything since then has been analysis and recommendations; I haven't changed the model in the code.

But Qwen is **not part of the default flow** anymore. There are two separate modes:

## Mode 1: continuity (what every user gets)
```
curl …/install.sh | sh -s -- fp_key
  └─ footprint login → saves key → context install
       ├─ Claude Code: SessionStart hook
       └─ OpenCode: plugin + /continue

New session → hook/plugin runs `footprint context`
  → reads your last Claude Code / OpenCode session in this project (local files)
  → injects goal, files, todos, last error, where you stopped
  → into whatever model you're using: Claude, Big Pickle, Gemini, GLM…
```
- **No Qwen, no training, no GPU, no heat.** It just reads files and adds text.
- The installer never downloads a model: `install.sh` only sets up Python files, and the `footprint` command only creates the model environment for `train`, `eval`, `serve` and `install`.

## Mode 2: local model (opt-in, still Qwen 1.5B)
Only if the user runs these on purpose:
```
footprint collect → footprint train → footprint install
  → sets up the model environment (mlx), downloads Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B
  → LoRA training on your transcripts (laptop heats up)
  → serves it at localhost:8399, shown in OpenCode as model "footprint"
```
This is the weak part covered earlier: undertrained, too small, and in a tool format OpenCode can't use.

## Summary
| | Today |
|---|---|
| Default user experience | Continuity only; works with any model; Qwen not involved |
| Qwen 1.5B | Still in the code, used only by the opt-in local mode |
| Recommended changes (not done) | Switch to Qwen3.8-27B or a 7–8B fallback, fix training, build the profile layer |

Should I make the switch now? Options:
- **(a)** Change the default to Qwen3.8-27B on 32GB+ Macs and a 7–8B model below that, plus the training fixes
- **(b)** Hide local model mode from the website and docs until it's good, and push the profile instead

| **Continuity (default)** | **Nothing in any model.** footprint *reads* your sessions and *writes text* | Your session files, added to the next prompt |
| **Profile (planned)** | Nothing in any model. One summary is written as a text file | `~/.footprint/` and your vault |

## How it "learns" without training
```
your sessions (local files)
   │  footprint reads them (plain Python, no AI)
   ▼
extracted text: goal, files touched, todos, last error, where you stopped
   │  added to the start of the next session
   ▼
Claude / Big Pickle / GLM / Gemini (unchanged, frozen models)
   → read it like a briefing note → act on it
```

Think of it like a **new colleague reading your handover notes** rather than going back to school. The model is already capable (Claude, GLM, etc.); footprint just gives it the right notes at the start.

**With the profile, it's the same idea with longer-lived notes:**
- footprint asks the model you already use to *summarise* your sessions into ~1–2k tokens of preferences, habits and stack facts. That's one ordinary request, not training.
- The file is saved and added to every new session alongside the handover.
- It's updated by re-summarising new sessions, again with no training.

## Why this beats training for footprint
- Works with **any** model, including Claude, which you can't fine-tune anyway.
- **Instant:** a new preference takes effect next session, with no retrain.
- **Transparent:** the user can read and edit exactly what the AI "knows" about them.
- **$0, no GPU, no heat.**

Training (LoRA) only makes sense when you want a model that behaves your way **without** being given these notes, like an offline local model. That's why it's opt-in.

content.text:
In this project, LoRA is used in exactly one place: the **opt-in local model mode**. Continuity (the default) doesn't use it.

## Where LoRA appears in the code

| Step | Command | File | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Data | `footprint collect` | `footprint_core/transcripts.py` | Your Claude transcripts → `data/train.jsonl` and `valid.jsonl` (each Claude reply becomes a training target) |
| 2. Train (Mac) | `footprint train` | `backends/mlx_backend.py` | `mlx_lm lora` on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-4bit, adapter width (rank) 8, 16 layers, lr 1e-5 → `adapters/adapters.safetensors` (21MB) |
| 2. Train (Linux/Windows) | `footprint train` | `backends/torch_backend.py` | `peft` `LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules="all-linear")` with TRL's `SFTTrainer` → `adapters/` |
| 3. Test | `footprint eval` | both backends | Loss and perplexity of base + adapter on the held-out data |
| 4. Serve | `footprint install` / `serve` | backends + `service.py` | Base model + adapter served at `127.0.0.1:8399/v1`, kept running by launchd or systemd |
| 5. Use | — | `service.py` `_opencode()` | Adds provider `footprint` to `opencode.json` and a `/footprint <task>` command in OpenCode |
| 6. Sync | `footprint sync push/pull` | `vault.py` | Copies `adapters/` and `data/` to your private GitHub vault (currently broken for users) |

```
transcripts → collect → train (LoRA on Qwen 1.5B) → adapters/ → serve :8399 → OpenCode "footprint" model
```

## Status
- It works end to end, but the adapter on this machine was trained for only **100 steps** (~2.5% of one pass over the data).
- The training data is wasteful: no `--mask-prompt`, so ~95% of the effort goes on non-Claude text.
- The base model is **too small** for agent work, and the **tool-call format** doesn't match what OpenCode expects.
- No user gets it unless they run `train` and `install` themselves; the curl installer and `login` never touch it.

**In short:** LoRA is an optional "personal offline model" feature that is plumbed in but not useful yet. Everything users get by default is the handover, with no LoRA involved.

content.text:
No, not in the same way. Without Qwen, footprint doesn't run or train any model. The other models are used **as they are**, by the coding tool, and footprint only adds text.

## The two ways a model can be used

| | Qwen (local mode) | Any other model (default) |
|---|---|---|
| Who runs the model | **footprint** (`mlx_lm server` on your Mac) | **The provider**: Anthropic, OpenCode Zen, Ollama cloud, Google… |
| Who picks it | `footprint install` adds the "footprint" model | You, in Claude Code or OpenCode (`/models`) |
| LoRA training | ✅ trained on your sessions | ❌ never trained |
| How footprint personalises it | Adapter weights + handover | **Handover text only** (profile later) |

```
Default (no Qwen):
  you → OpenCode / Claude Code → Big Pickle / Claude / GLM / Gemini (unchanged)
                     ▲
          footprint plugin adds the handover text at session start

Local mode (Qwen):
  you → OpenCode → model "footprint" → localhost:8399 → Qwen 1.5B + your LoRA
                     ▲
          footprint plugin adds the handover text too
```

## Could we LoRA other models the same way?
| Model | LoRA possible? |
|---|---|
| **Other open models you run locally** (Qwen3.8-27B, gpt-oss, Devstral…) | ✅ Same pipeline. Just change the model: `FOOTPRINT_MODEL=<mlx model id> footprint train` |
| **Open models in someone's cloud** (GLM-5.3 on Ollama cloud, Big Pickle) | ❌ The weights are on their servers; you can't attach an adapter |
| **Closed models** (Claude, GPT, Gemini) | ❌ No access to the weights |
| **Open models on Together / Fireworks** | ✅ Hosted multi-LoRA (paid, the enterprise path) |

**In short:** without Qwen, footprint is a **memory layer**: it reads your past sessions and briefs whatever model you use. The model itself stays the same. LoRA is only possible for open models you run yourself, locally or on hosted GPUs.

content.text:
Yes, but the "training" has to live **outside the model**, as text the model reads, because you can't change the weights of Claude, GLM on Ollama cloud, or Big Pickle. Some ways to make any model act on your past sessions, strongest first:

## 1. Session memory, retrieval-based ⭐ (best option)
Instead of baking sessions into weights, **search them when you need them**:
```
new task: "add a date picker limit"
  → footprint searches all your past sessions (local index)
  → finds: "dropdown 2005–2012 in dob-picker.tsx" session
  → injects: how it was solved, which files, what you corrected
  → any model gets those examples alongside the task
```
- This is what LoRA was trying to do, done better: the model sees **exact past solutions**, not a fuzzy average.
- Works with **every** model, updates instantly, and you can trace where each example came from.
- Cheap: a plain keyword search (Python standard library) is enough to start; add embeddings later.

## 2. Profile (already planned)
A summary of preferences, habits and stack, added to every session. Covers the *style* that LoRA teaches, for any model.

## 3. Learned skills / commands
Turn workflows you repeat across sessions into reusable instructions: "how this user deploys", "how they write tests", "their PR checklist".
- Written as `AGENTS.md` sections, Claude skills, or OpenCode commands.
- Any agent can follow them.

## 4. Local proxy (applies 1–3 to every request automatically)
```
OpenCode / any tool → footprint proxy (localhost) → any provider (Zen, Ollama, OpenRouter, Gemini…)
                         adds profile + retrieved examples to each request
```
- Personalisation then works per request, not just at session start, and with any OpenAI-compatible model.
- Claude Code already gets it through the hook, so it doesn't need the proxy.

## 5. LoRA, only for open models you host
Still possible for Qwen and similar models, locally or on Together or Fireworks, as an extra on top of 1–4.

## Summary
| Approach | Any model | Cost | Heat | What it captures |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Handover (have) | ✅ | $0 | none | last session |
| **Session memory** | ✅ | $0 | none | **how past tasks were solved** |
| Profile | ✅ | $0 | none | preferences, style |
| Skills | ✅ | $0 | none | repeated workflows |
| Proxy | ✅ (OpenAI-style) | $0 | none | applies the above per request |
| LoRA | open models only | GPU | 🔥 | style, in the weights |

**Recommendation:** build **Session memory + Profile**. That gives "any model, but it knows how I work", which was the goal of LoRA, without training or GPUs, and it works with Claude too.

def install():
    """Claude Code SessionStart hook + OpenCode plugin (auto) + /continue command (manual)."""
    path = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/settings.json")
    try:
        cfg = json.load(open(path, encoding="utf-8")) if os.path.exists(path) else {}
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        sys.exit(f"{path} is not valid JSON — fix it first, not overwriting")
    cmd = f'"{sys.executable}" "{config.ENTRY}" context'
    starts = cfg.setdefault("hooks", {}).setdefault("SessionStart", [])
    starts[:] = [e for e in starts if not any("footprint.py\" context" in h.get("command", "")
                                              for h in e.get("hooks", []))]
    starts.append({"matcher": "startup|clear", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": cmd}]})
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True)
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(cfg, f, indent=2)
    plugin = os.path.join(config.OPENCODE, "plugins", "footprint.js")
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(plugin), exist_ok=True)
    src = open(PLUGIN_SRC, encoding="utf-8").read()
    with open(plugin, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(src.replace("__PY__", json.dumps(sys.executable)).replace("__ENTRY__", json.dumps(config.ENTRY)))
    oc = os.path.join(config.OPENCODE, "commands", "continue.md")
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(oc), exist_ok=True)
    with open(oc, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("---\ndescription: continue from your last session in this project, Claude Code or OpenCode (footprint)\n---\n"

content.text:
Session memory is built and working. On every prompt, in both Claude Code and OpenCode, footprint adds the most similar past tasks from all your sessions: what you asked, files touched, commands run, and how it ended. It works with any model, needs no training or GPU, and doesn't heat the laptop.

I tested it end to end on your machine. In a real OpenCode run, Big Pickle got the memory and answered from it: "a DOB picker defaulting to 2005".

**How it works:**
```
your prompt
  → footprint recall   (local index of 692 past tasks, ~0.1s)
  → top 1–3 similar past tasks, only if they really match
  → Claude Code: added by a hook · OpenCode: hidden part of your message
  → the model sees how you solved it before
```

**Results on your real sessions:**
- *"limit the date picker dropdown years"* found your real DOB-picker task from `preproute`, 122 days ago in OpenCode, with the file, the commit, and the outcome.
- *"connect notion mcp server"* found your Notion sessions in both tools.
- *"ok push it"* and *"great thanks"* got nothing, as intended.
- Building the index the first time took 4.5s; after that it updates incrementally in about 0.1s per prompt.

**Safeguards:**
- Secrets (API keys, tokens, `KEY=` lines) are removed from the index.
- A match must share 2 or more words with the past task's prompt or file names.
- The same memory isn't repeated twice in one session.
- The current session is excluded.
- In OpenCode, the system prompt stays the same, so prompt caching keeps working.

**Fixed along the way:** `<task-notification>` and `<bash-…>` system messages were showing up as your "asks" in the handover too. Both are now filtered.

**Your machine:** I installed it here, so your Claude Code now runs the new hook on each prompt. If you want to roll back, the previous `settings.json` and plugin are saved in `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-aman-Developer-footprint/f03b4ca7-e5b0-487b-9917-bd2897564c5f/scratchpad/`.

Committed as `c808af9`, **not pushed**. The installer pulls straight from `main`, so pushing turns this on for every user who installs or updates. Should I push it? `alternateApproach.md` is still uncommitted too; it can go in the same push.

**Known limits:** it matches words, not meaning, so "auth" won't find "login". Embeddings can be added later if that becomes a problem. It also covers Claude Code and OpenCode only.

lastPrompt: how will it upgrade the benchmark of existing model ?

content.text:
**It won't change public benchmark scores.** SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench and the like are tasks the model has never seen in your history, so memory finds nothing relevant and adds nothing. On those, GLM-5.3 with footprint scores the same as GLM-5.3 without it.

What it can improve is a **personal benchmark**: how well a model does on *your* work, which is mostly repeats and variations of things you've done before.

## Where memory helps a model
| Without memory | With memory |
|---|---|
| Searches the repo to find the date-picker file | Already knows `dob-picker.tsx` |
| Guesses your conventions (npm or pnpm, test command, commit style) | Sees the exact commands you ran: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `git commit -m …` |
| Repeats a mistake you already corrected last time | Sees how it ended, including the fix |
| Re-learns the project's setup (Vercel, Neon, OAuth) every session | Gets the past solution in about 300 tokens |

So the gains show up as **fewer steps, fewer tokens, fewer wrong turns, and a higher success rate on repeated kinds of work**. A weaker model with your past solutions can close part of the gap to a stronger one *on those tasks*. It won't get smarter in general.

## How to measure it honestly
Nothing has been measured yet. The way to measure it is a replay test using your own history:
1. Pick about 20 past tasks whose result can be checked: a commit was made, tests passed, a file changed in a known way.
2. For each one, check out the repo **as it was before that task**, and give the original prompt to the model in a fresh session.
3. Run it twice: **without** memory, then **with** memory, excluding that task itself from the index so it can't just copy the answer.
4. Score each run on whether it succeeded (tests and type check pass, or the diff matches the real fix), plus steps, tokens and time.
5. Compare models too: Big Pickle and GLM-5.3, each with and without memory, against Claude without memory.

```
                      success   steps   tokens
big-pickle            ?/20       ?       ?
big-pickle + memory   ?/20       ?       ?
glm-5.3 + memory      ?/20       ?       ?
claude (reference)    ?/20       ?       ?
```

That table is the real claim: "your free model + footprint gets X% closer to Claude on your own work". It's what you'd put on the website, and it also decides whether memory, profile or LoRA is worth investing in (the gate in `alternateApproach.md`).

Want me to build this replay test (`footprint bench`)? It runs OpenCode headless with `opencode run`, so it costs nothing on free models.

## What footprint is, in one line
**When Claude runs out, you switch to a free model and keep working, and the new model already knows what you were doing and how you work.**

## The problem
You're halfway through a task in Claude Code and hit the limit. You open OpenCode with a free model, and it knows nothing:
- what you were building
- which files you changed
- what broke last
- how you like things done

You spend 20 minutes re-explaining, and the weaker model still makes mistakes Claude had already avoided.

## What footprint gives
Think of it as a **handover note plus a diary**, passed automatically to whichever model takes over.

**1. Handover note (continuity).** When you open a new session in any tool, footprint briefs the model:
> "You were adding the date-picker limit. Files: `dob-picker.tsx`. Last error: type check failed on line 42. Next step: run tests."

The new model picks up mid-task instead of starting cold.

**2. Diary (session memory, new).** On every message, footprint searches all your past Claude sessions and adds anything similar:
> "Last time you did something like this, you edited these files, ran these commands, and it ended like this."

The weaker model copies **Claude's earlier solution** instead of guessing.

**3. Same chat in another tool (`footprint switch`).** It moves the whole Claude conversation into OpenCode, message by message.

## How this makes another model perform better
We **don't change the model** and do no training. We change **what it knows when it starts**.

A weaker model fails mostly because it lacks context, not because it's dumb. It doesn't know your project, your past fixes, or where you stopped. footprint gives it notes that come from Claude's own work, so it:
- skips the exploring Claude already did
- follows the conventions Claude already learned
- avoids mistakes Claude already fixed

Analogy: a junior developer with the senior's notes finishes the senior's task much better than one starting from zero, even though the junior isn't as skilled.

**Honest limit:** it makes the free model much better at **continuing your work**. It won't make it as smart as Claude on brand-new hard problems.

## What the user does
1. Sign in at tracefootprint.space with GitHub and copy the key.
2. Paste one command in the terminal.
3. Keep working. When Claude is out, open OpenCode, and it continues.

**Price:** free. Everything runs on the user's machine, no GPU, and no data stored on our servers.

## The pitch
> **"Claude ran out? Keep going. footprint hands your work, and how Claude solved it, to any model."**

The search turned up good coverage of Unsloth's MoE fine-tuning on NVIDIA GPUs, but nothing confirming that MLX LoRA training works for MoE models.

**MLX side:** Unsloth's latest release notes mention MLX MoE models too big for memory keep experts on SSD, so Qwen3.8-Flash-Next runs on a 32 GB Mac. That describes running models, not training them. The notes also say MLX MoE models too big for your Mac keep experts on SSD, with slower replies. I found no source confirming LoRA fine-tuning on MLX.

**Supported MoE models (CUDA):** Unsloth's docs list gpt-oss, Qwen3 (30B, 235B, VL, Coder), DeepSeek R1, V3 and GLM (4.6, 4.7, Flash). The Qwen3.5 guide adds the Qwen3.5 model family (0.8B, 2B, 4B, 9B, 27B, 35B‑A3B, 122B‑A10B).

**Memory requirements:**
- Qwen3-30B-A3B: 16-bit LoRA uses 63GB. Unsloth's Qwen3 guide says it fine-tunes the 30B‑A3B model with just 17.5 GB VRAM. The gap likely reflects quantization, but the sources don't say so explicitly.
- Qwen3.5-35B-A3B: bf16 LoRA works on 74GB VRAM. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B: bf16 LoRA works on 256GB VRAM.
- gpt-oss: QLoRA requirements: gpt-oss-20b = 14GB VRAM • gpt-oss-120b = 65GB VRAM. BF16 LoRA requirements: gpt-oss-20b = 44GB VRAM • gpt-oss-120b = 210GB VRAM.

**Caveats:** Unsloth's guide says MoE QLoRA 4‑bit is not recommended due to BitsandBytes limitations, so bf16 LoRA is the recommended route for MoE models. The sources are unofficial aggregators or docs of mixed dates, so the figures may have changed.

Qwen3.8-27B is a dense 27B vision-language model released under Apache-2.0, and Qwen reports strong SWE-bench Pro results. The search didn't surface anything specific about fine-tuning terms.

- **Release and license:** Qwen says the weights went to Hugging Face and ModelScope on 2026-08-14. The Hugging Face FP8 README lists the license: apache-2.0. A third-party spec table notes that training data and full recipe are not published.
- **SWE-bench Pro:** Qwen's official figure is 61.7, versus 53.5 for Qwen3.6-27B and 53.4 for Claude Opus 4.6 Max. Qwen says these runs used the Claude Code harness, temp=1.0, top_p=0.95, and a 256K context window. One secondary source also notes Qwen used a refined task set with corrected problematic tasks, so the score isn't directly comparable to standard leaderboard runs.
- **Other coding benchmarks:** Terminal-Bench 2.1 is reported at 73.0 (up from 63.4), and a secondary blog reports DeepSWE at 42.2. These come from blog write-ups, not the primary model card.
- **Fine-tuning:** None of the results addressed fine-tuning directly. Community fine-tunes already exist, such as an uncensored variant on Hugging Face, but I found no official fine-tuning guidance.
- **Caveat:** The "90.0% on SWE-bench Verified" figure in one Hugging Face discussion is an independent, unofficial claim about Qwen3.6-27B, not Qwen3.8-27B, so don't treat it as a Qwen3.8 result.

The search turned up a few recent results on distilling open models from agent trajectories, mostly around Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-Coder.

- **Open-SWE-Traces (2026):** The strongest result. Fine-tuning Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B on this trajectory dataset reports 61.7% on SWE-bench Verified. The base Qwen3-Coder model scored 51.6%, a gain of roughly 10 points. On the SWE-bench Verified benchmark, the OPEN-SWE-AGENT achieved a resolved rate of 61.7% in the "no-think" setting and 59.3% in the "think" setting. Compared to the base Qwen3-Coder model's performance of 51.6%, this represents an absolute gain of roughly 10.1%. The ACL Findings version gives a slightly different headline number: 60% on SWE-bench Verified, 46.2% on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 36.8% on SWE-bench Pro. The arXiv version reports 57.1% on Multilingual, so check which version you're citing.
- **Including failed trajectories helped:** On Multilingual, the authors say including "unresolved" trajectories (where the agent tried but failed to find a fix) was beneficial. Their reported jump is from 49.6% to 57.1% when including the full corpus rather than just the successful patches.
- **Smaller-scale data still moves the needle:** In SWE-Bench++, fine-tuning on just 145 of these trajectories improves cross-lingual performance from 1.6% to 3.6% on SWE-bench Multilingual.
- **Older SFT baseline:** Kimi-Dev reports that the publicly available SWE-Agent trajectories were used to fine-tune its model, which reached 48.6% on SWE-bench Verified. Its training data came from 5,016 SWE-Agent trajectories collected with Claude 3.7 Sonnet in the SWE-smith set.
- **RL alternative:** A Modal overview notes that models trained entirely with RL, without supervised fine-tuning, can achieve competitive performance, citing DeepSWE-Preview at 59% with test-time scaling.

Caveat: the figures come from search snippets and papers that report different settings (thinking vs. no-thinking, test-time scaling, harness). Compare them only within the same harness and benchmark variant.

content.text:
Short version: **training on one user's sessions won't raise benchmark scores. Training on a large, curated pool of agent sessions does, by about 10 points in published work.** There's also a legal risk with Claude's terms, covered at the end.

## 1. What published work shows

| Study | Base model | Training data | Result (SWE-bench Verified) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Open-SWE-Traces** (NVIDIA, 2026) | Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B | Large curated set of agent sessions | **51.6% → 61.7%**, about +10 points ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.16038v1), [dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Open-SWE-Traces)) |
| Kimi-Dev | its own base | 5,016 SWE-Agent sessions recorded with Claude 3.7 Sonnet | 48.6% ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.23045)) |
| SWE-Bench++ | — | only **145** sessions | Multilingual 1.6% → 3.6%, so small data moves it only a little ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17419)) |
| DeepSWE | — | reinforcement learning, no supervised training | 59% ([Modal](https://modal.com/resources/best-open-source-models-swe-bench-coding-agents)) |

**Lessons:**
- **Data volume and quality are what matter.** The gains came from thousands of *verified* sessions across many repos.
- **Failed attempts helped too:** including them raised Multilingual from 49.6% to 57.1%.
- One user has about 700 tasks, mostly unverified. That's enough to teach **style**, not enough to raise **benchmark scores**.

## 2. Candidate models for fine-tuning

### Laptop SLMs (8–16GB RAM): learn style, weak as agents
| Model | Notes |
|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B / Qwen3.5-9B | Best in the 7–9B class on HumanEval; Qwen3.5-9B is about 6.6GB at 4-bit ([labellerr](https://www.labellerr.com/blog/best-small-language-models-under-10b-parameters/), [vdf](https://vdf.ai/blog/best-local-llm-for-coding/)) |
| Granite 4.1 8B (IBM) | HumanEval 87.2% |
| GLM-4.7-Flash | 59.2% SWE-bench Verified claimed for 5–8GB machines; size not stated ([promptquorum](https://www.promptquorum.com/local-llms/best-local-llms-for-coding)) |

No model under 10B had a SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench score in the sources. They're fine for autocomplete-level work and style, not for agent tasks.

### 32GB Mac or one 24GB GPU: the sweet spot ⭐
| Model | Base score (vendor) | License | Fine-tuning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3.8-27B** (dense) | SWE-bench Pro **61.7**, Terminal-Bench 2.1 **73.0** ([Qwen GitHub](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3.8), [HF](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8/raw/main/README.md)) | Apache-2.0 | Dense, so the easiest to train with LoRA (MLX or PEFT) |
| **Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B** (MoE) | 51.6% → **61.7%** Verified after session training | Apache-2.0 | **Proven fine-tuning target** with a public recipe; Unsloth fits it in ~17.5GB VRAM ([Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/faster-moe)) |
| Devstral Small 2 (24B) | 68.0% Verified | check | Dense, fits a 32GB Mac ([insiderllm](https://insiderllm.com/guides/best-local-coding-models-2026/)) |
| gpt-oss-20b | — | Apache-2.0 | QLoRA in 14GB VRAM ([Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/gpt-oss-how-to-run-and-fine-tune)) |

### Servers only (hosted training)
| Model | Training memory |
|---|---|
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B | bf16 LoRA ~256GB VRAM ([Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/qwen3.5/fine-tune)) |
| gpt-oss-120b | QLoRA 65GB, bf16 LoRA 210GB |
| GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 | Best open-weight models, but too large to fine-tune practically; use them as-is |

### Training tools
| Tool | Hardware | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **MLX** (current footprint) | Mac | Works for dense models; **training MoE models on MLX isn't confirmed** |
| **Unsloth** | NVIDIA GPU | Supports MoE models (12× faster); recommends bf16 LoRA for MoE, since 4-bit QLoRA is limited there |
| PEFT / TRL (current torch backend) | Any GPU | Standard; slower |

## 3. ⚠️ Legal risk: training on Claude's outputs
Anthropic's terms restrict using its services to **develop or train competing AI models**.
- **Pooling Claude sessions from many users to train a commercial "footprint model"** is high risk.
- Even per-user LoRA training sold as a product is a grey area.
- **Have a lawyer check this before building any training product on Claude sessions.**

Lower-risk options:
- Train on **public datasets** such as Open-SWE-Traces (check its licence), SWE-smith, or SWE-Gym.
- Keep Claude sessions for **memory and profile** (no training), which is what footprint does now.

## 4. Recommendation
| Goal | Do this |
|---|---|
| Best benchmark score for "Claude ran out" | Use **GLM-5.3 / Kimi K3 / Qwen3.8-27B as-is**, plus footprint memory. No training. |
| Best local model (32GB) | **Qwen3.8-27B**: highest base score, Apache-2.0, dense so LoRA is easy |
| Proven "+10 points from training" | **Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B** + Open-SWE-Traces-style data, trained with Unsloth on one GPU. That gives a footprint base model, with no Claude data needed. |
| Per-user personalisation | Memory + profile, as now. LoRA only for style, optional. |

**Next step:** build `footprint bench` (the replay test from earlier) and run *Qwen3.8-27B as-is*, *+ memory*, and *+ LoRA* on your own tasks. That will show whether training adds anything beyond memory.

Yes. For any practical model training you need a GPU.

| Hardware | Training possible? |
|---|---|
| **NVIDIA GPU** (CUDA) | ✅ Standard: Unsloth, PEFT |
| **Apple Silicon** (M1–M4) | ✅ Has a built-in GPU, which MLX uses (footprint's current Mac path). Model size is limited by memory: your 8GB M1 manages ~1.5–3B only. |
| **CPU only** (your Windows i5 laptop) | ⚠️ Technically possible, but ~10–100× slower: hours to days even for a tiny model, with heavy heat |
| **Intel integrated graphics** (Iris Xe) | ❌ Not usable for training in practice |

How big the GPU needs to be depends on the model:

| Model | GPU memory for LoRA (approx.) |
|---|---|
| 1.5–3B | 4–8GB |
| 7–8B | ~10–16GB (QLoRA); free Colab T4 works |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B | ~17.5GB (Unsloth) |
| Qwen3.8-27B | ~24GB+ |

**For footprint, though, the main feature (memory + handover) doesn't train anything, so it needs no GPU.** A GPU is only needed if you decide to offer trained models later, as a paid or hosted feature.

content.text:
Yes, your Mac can't do it, so rent a GPU. My pick: **RunPod**. It's the simplest to get going, has ready-made Unsloth and PyTorch templates, bills by the hour, and has GPUs from small to large.

**Which GPU to rent on RunPod:**
| Goal | GPU | Price (approx.) | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| First experiment | **RTX 4090 (24GB)** | ~$0.34/hr Community, ~$0.69–0.74/hr Secure | LoRA on 7–8B models; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B with Unsloth (~17.5GB) |
| Bigger model | **L40S (48GB)** | ~$0.99/hr | Qwen3.8-27B LoRA comfortably |
| Serious runs | A100 80GB | ~$1.19–1.39/hr | 30B+ models, faster |

**Free ways to start before paying:**
- **Google Colab (free T4):** fine for one 7–8B test run.
- **Modal:** $30 of free credits every month, billed per second. Good for small runs, but it's built mainly for serving models, so it's less convenient for long training.

**Alternatives:**
- **Vast.ai:** cheapest (4090 from ~$0.13–0.50/hr), but GPUs are rented from individuals, so less reliable.
- **Lambda:** reliable H100s (~$3.99/hr); overkill for now.

**What one footprint training run might cost (rough estimate):** your ~4k examples on an 8B model on a 4090 is probably about 1–2 hours, so roughly **$1–2 per run**. A 27–30B model on an L40S is maybe 2–4 hours, around **$2–4**. Measure on the first run.

**Suggested path:**
1. **Free Colab:** train Qwen3-8B on your `train.jsonl` with Unsloth, as a proof of concept.
2. **RunPod 4090:** Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B or Qwen3.8-27B for a real test.
3. Compare in `footprint bench` against *the same model without training, plus memory*. Only if training wins is it worth building into the product.

These prices come from third-party comparison sites and change often, so check RunPod's pricing page before you start.

content.text:
Yes, in three ways. Most useful first:

## 1. A free source of models for users ✅
**build.nvidia.com** offers 100+ models through an **OpenAI-style API** (`https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1`), with a free key:
- Limit of about **40 requests/min** per key; you can ask for 200
- It works in **OpenCode** like any other provider, so footprint's handover and memory work with it out of the box
- Model names include the vendor, e.g. `vendor/model`

**Catch:** according to the forums, the free tier is for **development and testing, not production**. So:
- ✅ Each user brings their own NVIDIA key, another free option alongside Big Pickle, Gemini and OpenRouter
- ✅ You use it to run `footprint bench` across many models for free
- ❌ Don't build your shared gateway on it

## 2. Serving per-team LoRA for enterprises ✅ (later, paid tier)
**NIM containers** run on your own or a customer's GPUs and can **serve a base model plus multiple LoRA adapters** ([NIM LoRA docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/large-language-models/2.1.4/advanced-use-cases/finetune-lora.html)). That's the multi-LoRA setup from the plan, packaged by NVIDIA.
- Good fit for enterprises that want everything **inside their own cloud**
- Licensing: as far as I know, it's free for development, and production needs an NVIDIA AI Enterprise licence. Confirm with NVIDIA.
- Alternatives: plain vLLM (free, more DIY), or Together and Fireworks (managed)

## 3. Training data ✅
NVIDIA's **Open-SWE-Traces** dataset is what lifted Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B from 51.6% to 61.7% in the research. It's public training data that avoids the Claude terms risk (check its licence).

## Where it doesn't help
- **Training:** NIM only serves models. Training is NVIDIA NeMo, or simply Unsloth on RunPod.
- **Your laptops:** NIM containers need NVIDIA GPUs.

**Quick win:** add NVIDIA as an option in the docs and Get Started page ("free models: Big Pickle, Gemini, OpenRouter, NVIDIA Build"). Want me to add a ready-to-copy `opencode.json` provider block for it?

Yes, for **small experiments**. It's not enough for the models that would really help.

**What a 16GB M2 can train (MLX LoRA):**
| Model | Feasible? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B / 3B (4-bit) | ✅ Comfortable | What footprint uses today; trains in minutes to an hour |
| **Qwen3-8B (4-bit)** | ⚠️ Tight but doable | Close other apps; batch 1, sequences up to 2048 tokens, gradient checkpointing. Likely several hours for a few thousand steps. |
| Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B | ❌ | Need 24GB+ just to train |

**Things to check on that Mac:**
- **Air or Pro?** An M2 **Air** has no fan, so it gets hot and slows down during long training. A **Pro** holds speed much better.
- **Free disk space:** needs about 10GB+ free for the model download, data and checkpoints.
- **Plugged in, and not in use while training:** close Chrome and the editor so all 16GB is available.

**How to run it (after fixing the training data):**
```sh
FOOTPRINT_MODEL=mlx-community/Qwen3-8B-4bit footprint collect
FOOTPRINT_MODEL=mlx-community/Qwen3-8B-4bit footprint train
```
I'd lower the sequence length to 2048 for 16GB, and the data fixes from earlier (`--mask-prompt`, train/test split by session, secret removal) **must** go in first. Otherwise hours of training go mostly into predicting tool output.

**Verdict:**
- ✅ Good for **proving the pipeline** and a first "does LoRA beat memory?" test on an 8B model, free.
- ❌ Not for the models that matter (27–30B). Use a **RunPod 4090 or L40S** for about $1–4 a run.
- Even after training, an 8B model on a 16GB Mac is slow for agent work, so judge it with `footprint bench`, not by feel.

content.text:
Using NVIDIA through **build.nvidia.com** won't exhaust your laptop, because the work happens on NVIDIA's servers.

There are two separate things here:

| | Where it runs | Laptop load |
|---|---|---|
| **build.nvidia.com API** (using their hosted models) | NVIDIA's cloud GPUs | ✅ None. Your laptop just sends text and gets text back, like using Claude. |
| **NIM containers** (self-hosted) | **Your own NVIDIA GPU** | ❌ Can't run on your Macs at all (needs an NVIDIA GPU) |
| **Training** | — | ⚠️ NIM **doesn't train**. It only *serves* models. NVIDIA's training tool is NeMo, which also needs NVIDIA GPUs. |

So:
- **You can't train with NIM**, on a laptop or anywhere; it isn't a training tool.
- **Using NVIDIA's hosted models** costs your laptop nothing, the same as Claude, Big Pickle or Gemini. With footprint memory on top, that's the no-heat setup.
- **If you want training without heating your laptop,** rent a cloud GPU: RunPod, Colab, or Modal. The laptop only uploads `train.jsonl`, and the training runs on their machines.

```
heats your laptop:   footprint train (MLX on your Mac)
no laptop heat:      NVIDIA API / Claude / Gemini (using models)
                     RunPod / Colab (training in the cloud)
```

content.text:
The way to measure this: **use the user's own Claude sessions as the answer key.** Replay those tasks with the user's chosen model, trained or not, and compare the result against what Claude actually did. That gives a "Claude parity score" for *their* work, whatever model they pick. Your memory surfaced the earlier plan for exactly this ("resume-a-task benchmark"); this is that plan, made concrete.

## `footprint bench`: how it works

```
1. HARVEST   from Claude sessions → tasks with a known good outcome
2. REPLAY    same prompt, same starting code → candidate model
3. SCORE     compare with Claude's result
4. REPORT    parity % per model
```

**1. Harvest the tasks (the answer key)**
- Pick Claude tasks that ended in a **git commit**; the commit hash is visible in the transcript (`[main abc123] …`).
- For each one, save:
  - the prompt
  - the repo and **the commit before** (the starting point)
  - **Claude's commit** (the reference answer)
  - **a check command** to verify the work: one Claude itself ran successfully (`npx tsc --noEmit`, `pytest`, `npm test`), or one detected from the project
- **Must be held out:** these sessions are never used for training or memory. Otherwise the model just copies the answer. This is the split-by-session fix again.

**2. Replay with any model**
- Create a clean git worktree at the starting commit.
- Run the candidate headless with the same prompt: `opencode run -m <provider/model> "<prompt>"`.
- Candidates can be anything: Big Pickle, GLM-5.3, an NVIDIA model, the user's trained LoRA (served on `localhost:8399`), with or without memory.

**3. Score each attempt**
| Score | How | Objective? |
|---|---|---|
| **Pass** | The check command passes | ✅ main score |
| **Same files** | Overlap between the files it changed and the files Claude changed | ✅ |
| **Equivalent?** | A strong model compares the two diffs: same / partial / wrong | ⚠️ helper only |
| **Cost** | Steps, tokens, time | ✅ |

**4. Report**
```
your tasks (20, held out)        pass   same-files  equivalent   steps
Claude (reference)               20/20     100%        —          12
qwen3.8-27b                      11/20      62%      9/20         19
qwen3.8-27b + your LoRA          13/20      70%     11/20         16
qwen3.8-27b + memory             14/20      74%     12/20         14
glm-5.3 + memory                 17/20      85%     15/20         13

Claude parity = candidate pass ÷ Claude pass   →  glm-5.3 + memory: 85%
```
*(Illustrative numbers, not measured.)*

That gives a defensible claim: **"on your own work, model X with footprint does Y% of what Claude did."** It also answers whether training beats memory for that user.

## Rules that keep it honest
- **Held-out tasks only:** never in training data or the memory index.
- **At least 20 tasks, each run 2+ times,** since models vary from run to run.
- **Pass/fail first;** the AI judge is only a tiebreaker.
- **Personal, not general.** It measures the user's own kind of work. For general ability, quote public benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench) separately; never claim "equals Claude" in general.
- **Runs locally:** the user's code never leaves their machine, apart from what the chosen model's provider sees.

## Cost and effort
- Using free models: $0. A trained model runs wherever it's served.
- Build effort: about a day for the first version (task harvest, replay through `opencode run`, pass/fail and file overlap, results table), with the AI judge added afterwards.

content.text: **2. `footprint bench`.** Writing it, with a self-check that builds a real throwaway git repo and a fake Claude transcript, so harvest, replay and scoring are tested without calling any model.

input.content:
"""Personal benchmark: how close does model X get to what Claude did, on *your* work?

Answer key = your own Claude Code sessions. A task qualifies when Claude ended
it with a git commit and ran a check (tsc / tests / lint / build) that passed.
Each candidate model gets the same prompt on a clean worktree of the commit
*before* Claude's, then the same check runs.

  footprint bench harvest [n]                      pick + validate held-out tasks (default 20)
  footprint bench run <provider/model>… [--memory on|off|both]
  footprint bench                                  show the latest report
  footprint bench upload                           send scores (numbers only) to your profile

Held-out sessions are excluded from memory and from `collect`, so no model can
copy the answer. Pass = check passes AND the model changed at least one file.
"""
import glob, json, os, re, shutil, subprocess, sys, tempfile, time

from . import config, context

HOME = os.path.expanduser("~/.footprint/bench")
TASKS = os.path.join(HOME, "tasks.json")
HOLDOUT = os.path.join(HOME, "holdout.txt")       # session ids kept out of memory + training
RESULTS = os.path.join(HOME, "results.json")
COMMIT = re.compile(r"\[[^\]\s]+(?: \(root-commit\))? ([0-9a-f]{7,40})\]")
CHECK = re.compile(r"\b(npx tsc\b.*--noEmit|tsc --noEmit|(?:npm|pnpm|yarn|bun) (?:run )?(?:test|lint|build|typecheck)\b"
                   r"|(?:python3? -m )?pytest\b|go test\b|cargo (?:test|check|build)\b|next build\b|ruff check\b)")
DEP_DIRS = ("node_modules", ".venv", "venv")      # ponytail: symlinked from the real repo; per-task installs if this proves flaky
RUN_TIMEOUT, CHECK_TIMEOUT = 900, 300


def holdout():
    return set(open(HOLDOUT).read().split()) if os.path.exists(HOLDOUT) else set()


def _git(cwd, *args):
    return subprocess.run(["git", "-C", cwd, *args], capture_output=True, text=True)


def _check_cmd(command, cwd, root):
    """Pull the check segment out of a chained Claude command -> (subdir relative to repo root, cmd)."""
    here = cwd
    for seg in re.split(r"&&|;|\|\|", command):
        seg = seg.split("|")[0].replace("2>&1", "").strip()
        if seg.startswith("cd "):
            here = os.path.normpath(os.path.join(here, os.path.expanduser(seg[3:].strip().strip("'\""))))
        elif CHECK.search(seg):
            rel = os.path.relpath(here, root)
            return (None if rel.startswith("..") else rel), seg
    return None, None


def _tasks_in(path):
    """Claude transcript -> candidate tasks: prompt, cwd, commit hash, check command."""
    sid, out, cur, pending = os.path.basename(path)[:-6], [], None, {}
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"):
        try:
            rec = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
        p = context._prompt(rec)
        if p:
            cur = {"sid": sid, "prompt": p, "cwd": rec.get("cwd"), "commit": None, "check": None}
            out.append(cur)
            continue
        content = (rec.get("message") or {}).get("content")
        if not cur or rec.get("isSidechain") or not isinstance(content, list):
            continue
        for b in content:
            if b.get("type") == "tool_use" and b.get("name") == "Bash":
                pending[b.get("id")] = (cur, (b.get("input") or {}).get("command", ""))
            elif b.get("type") == "tool_result" and b.get("tool_use_id") in pending:
                task, cmd = pending.pop(b["tool_use_id"])
                text = context.transcripts._text([b])
                if "git commit" in cmd and (m := COMMIT.search(text)):
                    task["commit"] = m.group(1)
                elif not b.get("is_error") and CHECK.search(cmd) and not task["check"]:
                    task["check"] = cmd
    return [t for t in out if t["commit"] and t["check"] and t["cwd"]]


def _worktree(root, rev):
    wt = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="fp-bench-")
    if _git(root, "worktree", "add", "--detach", "-f", wt, rev).returncode:
        shutil.rmtree(wt, ignore_errors=True)
        return None
    for d in DEP_DIRS:  # deps aren't in git; borrow the real repo's
        for src in glob.glob(os.path.join(root, d)) + glob.glob(os.path.join(root, "*", d)):
            dst = os.path.join(wt, os.path.relpath(src, root))
            if os.path.isdir(os.path.dirname(dst)) and not os.path.exists(dst):
                os.symlink(src, dst)
    return wt


def _drop(root, wt):
    _git(root, "worktree", "remove", "--force", wt)
    shutil.rmtree(wt, ignore_errors=True)


def _run_check(wt, task):
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(task["check_cmd"], shell=True, cwd=os.path.join(wt, task["check_dir"]),
                           capture_output=True, timeout=CHECK_TIMEOUT)
        return r.returncode == 0
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return False


def harvest(argv=()):
    """Newest qualifying tasks whose check really passes at Claude's commit -> held-out set."""
    n = int(argv[0]) if argv and argv[0].isdigit() else 20
    found, seen = [], set()
    files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(config.PROJECTS, "*", "*.jsonl")), key=os.path.getmtime, reverse=True)
    for f in files:
        for t in _tasks_in(f):
            root = _git(t["cwd"], "rev-parse", "--show-toplevel").stdout.strip() if os.path.isdir(t["cwd"]) else ""
            if not root or t["commit"] in seen:
                continue
            parent = _git(root, "rev-parse", f"{t['commit']}^").stdout.strip()
            t["check_dir"], t["check_cmd"] = _check_cmd(t["check"], t["cwd"], root)
            if not parent or not t["check_cmd"]:
                continue
            t.update(root=root, parent=parent,
                     claude_files=_git(root, "diff", "--name-only", parent, t["commit"]).stdout.split())
            wt = _worktree(root, t["commit"])
            ok = wt and _run_check(wt, t)
            if wt:
                _drop(root, wt)
            if ok and t["claude_files"]:
                seen.add(t["commit"])
                found.append(t)
                print(f"  ✓ {os.path.basename(root)} {t['commit'][:7]}  {t['prompt'][:70]!r}")
            if len(found) >= n:
                break
        if len(found) >= n:
            break
    os.makedirs(HOME, exist_ok=True)
    json.dump(found, open(TASKS, "w"), indent=1)
    open(HOLDOUT, "w").write("\n".join(sorted({t["sid"] for t in found})) + "\n")
    print(f"{len(found)} held-out tasks -> {TASKS}\n(their sessions are now excluded from memory + collect)")
    if len(found) < 5:
        print("few tasks: the bench needs Claude sessions that ran a check and ended in a git commit")


def opencode_runner(model, prompt, wt, env):
    t = time.time()
    subprocess.run(["opencode", "run", "-m", model, prompt], cwd=wt, env=env,
                   capture_output=True, timeout=RUN_TIMEOUT)
    return time.time() - t


def _tokens(wt):
    """Tokens OpenCode recorded for the session run in this worktree (0 if unknown)."""
    try:
        import sqlite3
        db = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{config.OPENCODE_DB}?mode=ro", uri=True)
        r = db.execute("select sum(tokens_input + tokens_output) from session where directory in (?, ?)",
                       (wt, os.path.realpath(wt))).fetchone()
        db.close()
        return int(r[0] or 0)
    except Exception:
        return 0


def run(argv, runner=opencode_runner):
    models = [a for a in argv if not a.startswith("--") and "/" in a]
    mode = next((a.split("=", 1)[1] for a in argv if a.startswith("--memory=")), "both")
    if not models:
        sys.exit("usage: footprint bench run <provider/model>… [--memory=on|off|both]")
    tasks = json.load(open(TASKS)) if os.path.exists(TASKS) else []
    if not tasks:
        sys.exit("no tasks. run: footprint bench harvest")
    rows = []
    for model in models:

                   r"|(?:python3? -m )?pytest\b|go test\b|cargo (?:test|check|build)\b|next build\b|ruff check\b)")

RUN_TIMEOUT, CHECK_TIMEOUT = 900, 300

    return set(open(HOLDOUT).read().split()) if os.path.exists(HOLDOUT) else set()

    here = cwd

            continue

            if b.get("type") == "tool_use" and b.get("name") == "Bash":
                pending[b.get("id")] = (cur, (b.get("input") or {}).get("command", ""))

    for seg in re.split(r"&&|;|\|\|", command):
        seg = seg.split("|")[0].replace("2>&1", "").strip()
        if seg.startswith("cd "):
            here = os.path.normpath(os.path.join(here, os.path.expanduser(seg[3:].strip().strip("'\""))))
        elif CHECK.search(seg):
            rel = os.path.relpath(here, root)
            return (None if rel.startswith("..") else rel), seg
    return None, None


def _tasks_in(path):
    """Claude transcript -> candidate tasks: prompt, cwd, commit hash, check command."""
    sid, out, cur, pending = os.path.basename(path)[:-6], [], None, {}
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"):
        try:
            rec = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
        p = context._prompt(rec)
        if p:
            cur = {"sid": sid, "prompt": p, "cwd": rec.get("cwd"), "commit": None, "check": None}
            out.append(cur)
            continue
        content = (rec.get("message") or {}).get("content")
        if not cur or rec.get("isSidechain") or not isinstance(content, list):
            continue
        for b in content:
            if b.get("type") == "tool_use" and b.get("name") == "Bash":
                pending[b.get("id")] = (cur, (b.get("input") or {}).get("command", ""))
            elif b.get("type") == "tool_result" and b.get("tool_use_id") in pending:
                task, cmd = pending.pop(b["tool_use_id"])
                text = context.transcripts._text([b])
                if "git commit" in cmd and (m := COMMIT.search(text)):
                    task["commit"] = m.group(1)
                elif not b.get("is_error") and CHECK.search(cmd) and not task["check"]:
                    task["check"] = cmd
    return [t for t in out if t["commit"] and t["check"] and t["cwd"]]


def _worktree(root, rev):
    wt = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="fp-bench-")
    if _git(root, "worktree", "add", "--detach", "-f", wt, rev).returncode:
        shutil.rmtree(wt, ignore_errors=True)
        return None
    for d in DEP_DIRS:  # deps aren't in git; borrow the real repo's
        for src in glob.glob(os.path.join(root, d)) + glob.glob(os.path.join(root, "*", d)):
            dst = os.path.join(wt, os.path.relpath(src, root))
            if os.path.isdir(os.path.dirname(dst)) and not os.path.exists(dst):
                os.symlink(src, dst)
    return wt


def _drop(root, wt):
    _git(root, "worktree", "remove", "--force", wt)
    shutil.rmtree(wt, ignore_errors=True)


def _run_check(wt, task):
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(task["check_cmd"], shell=True, cwd=os.path.join(wt, task["check_dir"]),
                           capture_output=True, timeout=CHECK_TIMEOUT)
        return r.returncode == 0
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return False


def harvest(argv=()):
    """Newest qualifying tasks whose check really passes at Claude's commit -> held-out set."""
    n = int(argv[0]) if argv and argv[0].isdigit() else 20
    found, seen = [], set()
    files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(config.PROJECTS, "*", "*.jsonl")), key=os.path.getmtime, reverse=True)
    for f in files:
        for t in _tasks_in(f):
            root = _git(t["cwd"], "rev-parse", "--show-toplevel").stdout.strip() if os.path.isdir(t["cwd"]) else ""
            if not root or t["commit"] in seen:
                continue
            parent = _git(root, "rev-parse", f"{t['commit']}^").stdout.strip()
            t["check_dir"], t["check_cmd"] = _check_cmd(t["check"], t["cwd"], root)
            if not parent or not t["check_cmd"]:
                continue
            t.update(root=root, parent=parent,
                     claude_files=_git(root, "diff", "--name-only", parent, t["commit"]).stdout.split())
            wt = _worktree(root, t["commit"])
            ok = wt and _run_check(wt, t)
            if wt:
                _drop(root, wt)
            if ok and t["claude_files"]:
                seen.add(t["commit"])
                found.append(t)
                print(f"  ✓ {os.path.basename(root)} {t['commit'][:7]}  {t['prompt'][:70]!r}")
            if len(found) >= n:
                break
        if len(found) >= n:
            break
    os.makedirs(HOME, exist_ok=True)
    json.dump(found, open(TASKS, "w"), indent=1)
    open(HOLDOUT, "w").write("\n".join(sorted({t["sid"] for t in found})) + "\n")
    print(f"{len(found)} held-out tasks -> {TASKS}\n(their sessions are now excluded from memory + collect)")
    if len(found) < 5:
        print("few tasks: the bench needs Claude sessions that ran a check and ended in a git commit")


def opencode_runner(model, prompt, wt, env):
    t = time.time()
    subprocess.run(["opencode", "run", "-m", model, prompt], cwd=wt, env=env,
                   capture_output=True, timeout=RUN_TIMEOUT)
    return time.time() - t


def _tokens(wt):
    """Tokens OpenCode recorded for the session run in this worktree (0 if unknown)."""
    try:
        import sqlite3
        db = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{config.OPENCODE_DB}?mode=ro", uri=True)
        r = db.execute("select sum(tokens_input + tokens_output) from session where directory in (?, ?)",
                       (wt, os.path.realpath(wt))).fetchone()
        db.close()
        return int(r[0] or 0)
    except Exception:
        return 0


def run(argv, runner=opencode_runner):
    models = [a for a in argv if not a.startswith("--") and "/" in a]
    mode = next((a.split("=", 1)[1] for a in argv if a.startswith("--memory=")), "both")
    if not models:
        sys.exit("usage: footprint bench run <provider/model>… [--memory=on|off|both]")
    tasks = json.load(open(TASKS)) if os.path.exists(TASKS) else []
    if not tasks:
        sys.exit("no tasks. run: footprint bench harvest")
    rows = []
    for model in models:
        for mem in {"on": [True], "off": [False]}.get(mode, [False, True]):
            env = {**os.environ, "FOOTPRINT_MEMORY": "on" if mem else "off"}
            passed, overlap, secs, toks = 0, 0.0, 0.0, 0
            for i, t in enumerate(tasks, 1):
                wt = _worktree(t["root"], t["parent"])
                if not wt:
                    continue
                try:
                    try:
                        secs += runner(model, t["prompt"], wt, env)
                    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                        secs += RUN_TIMEOUT
                    changed = set(_git(wt, "diff", "--name-only", "HEAD").stdout.split()) | {
                        l[3:] for l in _git(wt, "status", "--porcelain").stdout.splitlines() if l.startswith("??")}
                    changed -= set(DEP_DIRS)
                    ok = bool(changed) and _run_check(wt, t)
                    ref = set(t["claude_files"])
                    overlap += len(changed & ref) / len(changed | ref) if changed | ref else 0
                    toks += _tokens(wt)
                    passed += ok
                    print(f"  [{model}{' +memory' if mem else ''}] {i}/{len(tasks)} {'PASS' if ok else 'fail'}  {t['prompt'][:60]!r}")
                finally:
                    _drop(t["root"], wt)
            n = len(tasks)
            rows.append({"model": model, "memory": mem, "passed": passed, "total": n,
                         "overlap": round(overlap / n, 3), "seconds": round(secs / n, 1), "tokens": toks // n})
    os.makedirs(HOME, exist_ok=True)
    hist = json.load(open(RESULTS)) if os.path.exists(RESULTS) else []
    hist.append({"date": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime()), "tasks": len(tasks), "rows": rows})
    json.dump(hist, open(RESULTS, "w"), indent=1)
    report()


def report(_=()):
    hist = json.load(open(RESULTS)) if os.path.exists(RESULTS) else []
    if not hist:
        sys.exit("no results yet. run: footprint bench harvest, then footprint bench run <provider/model>")
    last = hist[-1]
    print(f"\nClaude parity — {last['tasks']} held-out tasks from your sessions · {last['date'][:10]}\n")
    print(f"{'model':<34}{'parity':>8}{'pass':>8}{'same files':>12}{'avg s':>8}{'tokens':>9}")
    print(f"{'Claude (reference)':<34}{'100%':>8}{last['tasks']:>5}/{last['tasks']:<2}{'100%':>12}")
    for r in sorted(last["rows"], key=lambda r: -r["passed"]):
        name = r["model"] + (" + memory" if r["memory"] else "")
        print(f"{name:<34}{r['passed'] * 100 // max(r['total'], 1):>7}%{r['passed']:>5}/{r['total']:<2}"
              f"{r['overlap'] * 100:>11.0f}%{r['seconds']:>8}{r['tokens']:>9}")


def upload(_=()):
    """Numbers only (model names, scores, counts, date) -> your profile. No prompts, code or diffs."""
    from . import vault
    hist = json.load(open(RESULTS)) if os.path.exists(RESULTS) else []
    if not hist:
        sys.exit("no results yet. run: footprint bench run <provider/model>")
    if not os.path.exists(vault.KEY_FILE):
        sys.exit("not signed in. run: footprint login fp_…")
    key = open(vault.KEY_FILE, encoding="utf-8").read().strip()
    code, r = vault._http(f"{vault.API}/api/bench", data=hist[-1], [redacted]
    if code != 200:
        sys.exit(f"upload failed ({code}): {r.get('error', '')}")
    print(f"uploaded — see {vault.API}/account")

content.text:
Here is the full list of models to use when Claude runs out, ranked by benchmark and grouped by how you'd run them. Numbers come from my earlier research; they're mostly vendor-reported and sources disagree, so treat them as rankings.

## Reference: Claude Opus 5.5
SWE-bench Pro **89.9%** (Anthropic-reported) · Terminal-Bench 4.0 **59.6–66.4%**

## 1. Closed frontier models: same level as Opus 5.5, paid
| Model | Level | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Fable 5.1 | Equal or above Opus 5.5 | Anthropic API (paid) |
| GPT-6 Astra | Comparable | OpenAI API (paid) |
| Gemini (latest) | Strong; free daily cap | Gemini CLI / AI Studio key (free tier) |

## 2. Best open-weight models in the cloud ⭐ main fallback candidates
| Rank | Model | Benchmark | Free / cheap access |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **GLM-5.3** | Top open model on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (~42 vs ~52 for Opus 5) | `ollama/glm-5.3:cloud` (free plan may not include it, test it) · GLM-5.3-Flash ~$0.15/$0.50 per 1M tokens |
| 2 | **Kimi K3** | ~10–20 points below Opus 5.5 on coding indexes | Moonshot API; free tier covers older K2.6 only |
| 3 | **DeepSeek V4.1** | BenchLM coding 62.9 vs 82.9 for Opus 5.5 | ~5M free tokens for new users, then ~$0.15–0.30 per 1M |
| 4 | **MiMo-V2.6-Pro** | Top open-weight on the Artificial Analysis index (46, ~12 below Opus 5.5) | API / OpenRouter |
| 5 | **GLM-5.2** | SWE-bench Pro 62.1 · Verified ~78.7 | Ollama cloud, OpenRouter |
| 6 | **MiniMax M2.5 / M3** | Verified 80.2 (M2.5) · Pro 59.0 (M3) | API / OpenRouter |
| — | **Big Pickle** | Not published | Free in OpenCode Zen, no setup |
| — | NVIDIA Build catalog | Many of the above | Free key, ~40 requests/min, development only |

## 3. Local models, by laptop RAM
| RAM | Best model | Benchmark | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8GB | Qwen3-4B / Qwen2.5-Coder-3B | — | Autocomplete level only; your M1 Air is here |
| 16GB | **Qwen3-8B / Qwen3.5-9B** | Best 7–9B on HumanEval | Your colleague's M2 and the Windows laptop; slow on CPU |
| 32GB | **Qwen3.8-27B** ⭐ | SWE-bench Pro **61.7**, Terminal-Bench 2.1 **73.0** | Best laptop model by far; Apache-2.0 |
| 32GB | Devstral Small 2 (24B) | Verified 68.0 | Strong agent model |
| 32GB | Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B | Verified 51.6 base | Fast (MoE design) |
| 48–64GB | Qwen3-Coder-Next | Verified ~71 | Closest local model to frontier |
| 128GB+ | gpt-oss-120b, GLM-4.5-Air | Strong | Workstation-class Macs |

## 4. Best models for fine-tuning (if you train later)
| Model | Why | Proven result |
|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B** | Public recipe and data; Unsloth fits it in ~17.5GB | **51.6% → 61.7%** Verified after training on agent sessions (Open-SWE-Traces) |
| **Qwen3.8-27B** | Highest base score, dense, so easiest to train with LoRA | No published fine-tune yet |
| gpt-oss-20b | Small, Apache-2.0 | QLoRA in 14GB |

## Recommendation for footprint users
| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Claude ran out, want free, no setup | **Big Pickle + footprint memory** |
| Want the best open model | **GLM-5.3** (`ollama/glm-5.3:cloud`, or Flash at ~$0.15/1M) + memory |
| Want the strongest free API | **Gemini** (daily cap) + memory |
| Offline or private, 32GB Mac | **Qwen3.8-27B** locally + memory |

Then measure which one is actually best **for you**, on your own tasks:
```sh
footprint bench run opencode/big-pickle ollama/glm-5.3:cloud --memory=both
```

Sources: [benchlm SWE-bench Pro](https://benchlm.ai/benchmarks/swe-bench-pro) · [benchlm Opus 5.5](https://benchlm.ai/models/claude-opus-5-5) · [llm-stats SWE-bench Pro](https://llm-stats.com/benchmarks/swe-bench-pro) · [morphllm best coding model](https://www.morphllm.com/best-ai-model-for-coding) · [morphllm open-source 2026](https://www.morphllm.com/best-open-source-coding-model-2026) · [Qwen3.8 GitHub](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3.8) · [Open-SWE-Traces](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.16038v1) · [insiderllm local models](https://insiderllm.com/guides/best-local-coding-models-2026/) · [digitalapplied self-host](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/best-open-weight-coding-models-self-host-hardware-match-2026) · [Unsloth MoE](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/faster-moe) · [morphllm LLM API prices](https://www.morphllm.com/llm-api)

Pushed. GitHub is at `80c99ac`, with nothing left uncommitted. The two commits were already made, so this was just the push.

| Commit | What |
|---|---|
| `8b895e1` | Memory: generic chat words no longer cause false matches |

Checked live after the deploy:
- **Vercel:** the deploy succeeded.
- **Upload endpoint:** `tracefootprint.space/api/bench` is up and answers 401 to a request without a key.
- **Badge:** `/api/badge/…` returns the "invalid link" badge for a bad link.
- **Fresh install:** a clean install from the website includes `footprint bench`, which prints "no results yet" until you run it.

To get your report onto your profile:
```sh
footprint bench harvest
footprint bench run opencode/big-pickle ollama/glm-5.3:cloud --memory=both
footprint bench upload
```
The upload needs `footprint login fp_…` with a key you generated after the key format change. Your old `macbook-test` key won't work.

The account page now has an **All commands** section, in five groups. I tested that all of them render on a local server (signed in with a test cookie).

| Group | Commands |
|---|---|
| **Inside your coding tool** | `/continue [next task]`, `/clear` |
| **Account & updates** | `footprint login fp_…`, re-run the install command to update |
| **Continuity & memory** | `context`, `context install`, `recall <text>`, `switch`, `switch list`, `switch <session-id>` |
| **Claude parity bench** | `bench harvest [n]`, `bench run <provider/model>… --memory=both`, `bench`, `bench upload` |
| **Local model (optional)** | `trace`, `collect`, `train`, `eval`, `install`, `serve`, `status`, with a note that it needs a 16GB+ Apple Silicon Mac or an NVIDIA GPU and heats the laptop |

- **Fixed:** `footprint status` was described as showing sign-in status. It actually shows the local model's state, and the page now says so.
- **Left out:** `footprint key` and `footprint sync` still need the old GitHub sign-in, which doesn't work for users. Keys are managed on the account page itself.

# footprint — New User Guide

Claude ran out? Keep going on a free model that already knows what you were doing.
Same steps as **Get started** on https://www.tracefootprint.space/account.

Steps 1–7 are required (about two minutes). 8–10 are optional.

---

## 1. Check you have Python 3

```sh
python3 --version
```

Nothing else needed — no npm, no git. macOS / Linux for now (Windows coming).
No Python on macOS? `xcode-select --install`.

## 2. Generate your key

1. Open https://www.tracefootprint.space/account → **Continue with GitHub** → **Authorize**.
   (footprint creates a private `footprint-vault` repo in your GitHub — your data lives there, not with us.)
2. Type a label (e.g. `macbook`) → **Generate API key**.
3. The key is shown **once**, with the install command already filled in. Copy that command.

## 3. Install + sign in

Paste the copied command in your terminal:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://www.tracefootprint.space/install.sh | sh -s -- fp_yourkey
```

Installs footprint into `~/.footprint/app`, signs you in, and hooks into Claude Code and OpenCode.

## 4. Open a new terminal and check it works

```sh
footprint context
```

Prints your last session in this folder — or "no previous session", which is fine on day one.

## 5. Get OpenCode (your free fallback)

```sh
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
```

Free coding agent with free models (Big Pickle). Skip if you have it.

## 6. Work in Claude Code as usual

```sh
cd my-project
claude
```

Nothing to change. footprint remembers each session: goal, files, todos, last error, how tasks were solved.

## 7. Claude ran out? Open OpenCode in the same project

```sh
cd my-project
opencode
```

- The new session already knows where you stopped.
- Every prompt also gets your **similar past work** from all your sessions — any model.
- Pick a model with `/models` (Big Pickle is free).
- Chat already open? Type `/continue`.

---

## 8. (Optional) Want the exact same chat instead?

```sh
footprint switch
```

Moves your whole Claude Code conversation into OpenCode, message by message.
`footprint switch list` shows session ids; `footprint switch <id>` opens a specific one.

## 9. (Optional) Measure which free model works best for you

```sh
footprint bench harvest
footprint bench run opencode/big-pickle --memory=both
footprint bench upload
```

Replays tasks Claude finished in your repos with any model and scores them.
Scores (numbers only — never prompts or code) appear under **Claude parity** on your account,
where you can create a public share link + README badge.

## 10. (Optional, advanced) Train a local model on your sessions

Needs an Apple Silicon Mac with 16GB+ (or an NVIDIA GPU) — it heats the laptop.

```sh
footprint trace      # first: only sessions from now on become training data
# …work for a while…
footprint collect
footprint train
footprint eval
footprint install    # keeps it running; shows up in OpenCode as "footprint"
```

---

## All commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/continue [next task]` | Inside OpenCode: pull the last session's state into a chat that was already open |
| `/clear` | Inside Claude Code: fresh chat that still starts with the last session's state |
| `footprint login fp_…` | Sign in on this device |
| re-run the install command | Update footprint (your data is kept) |
| `footprint context` | Preview what the next session will be handed |
| `footprint context install` | (Re)install the Claude Code hooks + OpenCode plugin |
| `footprint recall <text>` | Similar past work footprint adds to a prompt like that |
| `footprint switch [list \| <id>]` | Open a Claude Code chat in OpenCode, full history |
| `footprint bench harvest [n]` | Pick tasks Claude finished as the answer key |
| `footprint bench run <provider/model>… --memory=both` | Replay them with any model |
| `footprint bench` / `bench upload` | Show the report / send scores to your account |
| `footprint setup` | One-time local model backend install (runs automatically) |
| `footprint trace` · `collect` · `train` · `eval` | Local model: arm tracing, build data, train, test |
| `footprint install` · `serve` · `status` | Local model: keep running, run by hand, show state |

## If something goes wrong

- **`footprint: command not found`** — open a new terminal (step 4).
- **"key rejected"** — revoked, mistyped, or made before 2 Nov 2026. Generate a new one on the account page.
- **No handover in a new session** — run `footprint context` in that folder. "No previous session" = nothing recent there yet.
- **Lost a key** — Revoke it on the account page; every machine using it stops.

Paste the copied command in your terminal:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://www.tracefootprint.space/install.sh | sh -s -- fp_yourkey
```

Installs footprint into `~/.footprint/app`, signs you in, and hooks into Claude Code and OpenCode.

## 4. Open a new terminal and check it works

```sh
footprint context
```

Prints your last session in this folder — or "no previous session", which is fine on day one.

## 5. Get OpenCode (your free fallback)

```sh
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
```

Free coding agent with free models (Big Pickle). Skip if you have it.

## 6. Work in Claude Code as usual

```sh
cd my-project
claude
```

Nothing to change. footprint remembers each session: goal, files, todos, last error, how tasks were solved.

## 7. Claude ran out? Open OpenCode in the same project

```sh
cd my-project
opencode
```

- The new session already knows where you stopped.
- Every prompt also gets your **similar past work** from all your sessions — any model.
- Pick a model with `/models` (Big Pickle is free).
- Chat already open? Type `/continue`.

---

## 8. (Optional) Want the exact same chat instead?

```sh
footprint switch
```

Moves your whole Claude Code conversation into OpenCode, message by message.
`footprint switch list` shows session ids; `footprint switch <id>` opens a specific one.

## 9. (Optional) Measure which free model works best for you

```sh
footprint bench harvest
footprint bench run opencode/big-pickle --memory=both
footprint bench upload
```

Replays tasks Claude finished in your repos with any model and scores them.
Scores (numbers only — never prompts or code) appear under **Claude parity** on your account,
where you can create a public share link + README badge.

## 10. (Optional, advanced) Train a local model on your sessions

Needs an Apple Silicon Mac with 16GB+ (or an NVIDIA GPU) — it heats the laptop.

```sh
footprint trace      # first: only sessions from now on become training data
# …work for a while…
footprint collect
footprint train
footprint eval
footprint install    # keeps it running; shows up in OpenCode as "footprint"
```

---

## All commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/continue [next task]` | Inside OpenCode: pull the last session's state into a chat that was already open |
| `/clear` | Inside Claude Code: fresh chat that still starts with the last session's state |
| `footprint login fp_…` | Sign in on this device |
| re-run the install command | Update footprint (your data is kept) |
| `footprint context` | Preview what the next session will be handed |
| `footprint context install` | (Re)install the Claude Code hooks + OpenCode plugin |
| `footprint recall <text>` | Similar past work footprint adds to a prompt like that |
| `footprint switch [list \| <id>]` | Open a Claude Code chat in OpenCode, full history |
| `footprint bench harvest [n]` | Pick tasks Claude finished as the answer key |
| `footprint bench run <provider/model>… --memory=both` | Replay them with any model |
| `footprint bench` / `bench upload` | Show the report / send scores to your account |
| `footprint setup` | One-time local model backend install (runs automatically) |
| `footprint trace` · `collect` · `train` · `eval` | Local model: arm tracing, build data, train, test |
| `footprint install` · `serve` · `status` | Local model: keep running, run by hand, show state |

## If something goes wrong

- **`footprint: command not found`** — open a new terminal (step 4).
- **"key rejected"** — revoked, mistyped, or made before 2 Nov 2026. Generate a new one on the account page.
- **No handover in a new session** — run `footprint context` in that folder. "No previous session" = nothing recent there yet.
- **Lost a key** — Revoke it on the account page; every machine using it stops.
